utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Registrar. Could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes. Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-03-68, the Prosecutor versus Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, and good afternoon. Mr. Oric, can you follow the proceedings in a language that you can understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours, ladies and gentlemen. I can follow the proceedings in my own mother tongue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. You may sit down. And good afternoon to you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours, and also good afternoon to my learned friends of the Defence. My name is Jan Wubben, lead counsel for the Prosecution. I'm here together with co-counsel, Ms. Patricia Sellers, Mr. Gramsci Di Fazio, Ms. Joanne Richardson, and our case manager, Mrs. Donnica Henry-Frijlink.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, and good afternoon to you and your team. Appearances for Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. I'm Vasvija Vidovic, and together with Mr. John Jones, I represent Mr. Naser Oric. We're joined by our legal assistant, Ms. Jasmina Cosic, and our case manager, Geoff Roberts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Any preliminaries? Mr. Wubben?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, last week an issue was raised regarding translation of a statement. I requested Ms. Patricia Sellers to prepare a submission in that respect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sellers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I believe last week Defence counsel used Defence Exhibit D135, and, during the course of their use of the exhibit, they referred to the translation and the problems in the English translations. And then Your Honour, Judge Agius, also mentioned that problems within the translation could no doubt cause further problems as you're looking at documents. We just wanted to return to the Trial Chamber on that issue to inform the Trial Chamber and to also remind Defence counsel that the documents that they used, which became D135, was turned over to them on receipt 11, both that B/C/S copy and an English copy, and that the English translation you received was not made by the Registry here or by any of the OTP services. As a matter of fact, they came up with the original document from its source in the former Yugoslavia. Because it was not one of our translations, we then put in for formal translation with the Registry service and that was served on the Defence counsel a few months later, as early as January 2004. And Your Honour, I state that to say that there was an official translation that was not being used by the Defence. The Trial Chamber and the Defence will have access to this official translation made by our services. And just lastly, I believe the Defence gave our attention that on December 16th, they did make mention of this problem in the record. We have checked the record. We have been unable to locate that mention. So if we could have further assistance on that, we would appreciate it, but we would like to inform the Court that the official translation is probably the best one to look at in terms of putting forward the evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Has the official translation been tendered?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, my impression is that the unofficial translation is part of D135, and not the official. We would say that if they would just go into their official translation, that that might resolve any issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Right. But it might or it may resolve the issue for the Defence, but what about the Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If there is an official translation, and we don't have it, we need it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is in essence what we lead to, that if that is not part of D135, that we might have to ask that the Prosecution submit just the translation in relationship, the official translations in relationship to D135.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Ms. Sellers. Let's not lose more time on this. May I suggest that you look into this further and that if the official translation is not in the records as yet, that you will have it brought forward or tendered at the earliest. With regard to the rest, I think -- I honestly don't think we ought to lose much more time. Try to sort it out amongst yourselves, whether it was mentioned on a previous occasion, when was that? I don't think we are interested in that for the time being. But let me send out the message loud and clear, what is of great concern to us as a Trial Chamber. Unless our attention is drawn to possible errors in translation of the hundreds of documents that have been tendered, we would not be aware of such errors. And we would rely on the documents as translated and as tendered. I would hate to think for a moment that after having gone through such a laborious exercise as we are bound to do later on, when we come to the final exercise, we rely on one or more particular document as translated and as tendered. We sadly find out at a later stage, after judgement has been delivered, that either you or the Defence would have found out that we were relying on a wrongly translated text. So this is our concern. I mean, we have hundreds of documents that have been translated, and we are not in a position, ourselves, to vet them, to check where the translation is accurate or not. We've had several instances here where the translation was pointed out to be incorrect. I don't know. I would take it on that score that there may be others. But if there are others that you are aware of, please do come forward and let us -- draw our attention to that. Because it would be tragic, literally tragic, having spent a year and a half on a trial, handing down a decision one way or another, only to find out that it was handed down, partly at least, on a translation which was not accurate.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution shares your concern and we'll act accordingly. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm sure you will. So any further preliminaries? Ms. Vidovic? You don't need to address this matter. So if there are any other preliminaries ...

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, just very briefly with respect to translations, because this is something that I've always seen as a huge problem from the very beginning. We always do our best to draw the Trial Chamber's attention to the accuracy of documents, but there is one document in particular in which there are quite a few mistakes. And from the very start, I think even the pre-trial stage, I did draw your attention to incorrect translations in many parts of the document P84, P84. I've done that on a number of occasions, and so far we have not received a corrected version. It is a very serious document, and I would like to take this opportunity to draw the Prosecutor's office attention once again to this matter. And we do need an official translation there, because as far as I can see, it was still using an unofficial or a draft translation of this. And this is a rather bulky document as well, and that's why we're calling the witness as well, who is the author of the document. But it would be better not to have to correct it in the course of the author's testimony, because it would take ages. So it would be better to check it out sooner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The difference between the two parties in this context is that while I can look at the Prosecutor -- at the Prosecution and demand a correct translation and expect from the Prosecution to provide the Trial Chamber with precise and correct and faithful translations, I cannot at the same time look at the Defence and call on them to point out any mistakes in the translations, because I simply cannot do that. They have a right to remain silent, even on -- in that context. So I do appreciate, Ms. Vidovic, you standing up and pointing out that you -- in your opinion, there are still inaccuracies in P84. Yes, Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, we will contact the Defence, because we will always support any change or any way to improve the translation. We will do that today already.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Last thing before we bring in the witness. I think you have been informed that we're trying to finish a little bit earlier today and instead of having two breaks, we'll have one break, which will be of 30 minutes, which will enable us to cover the same territory but finish half an hour earlier. All right? So, Mr. Buric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Good afternoon to you, Mr. Buric.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I hope you had a good weekend, during which hopefully you rested, because you have got two days now of cross-examination. But before we arrive at the cross-examination, we still have about 20 minutes, I understand, or half an hour, of examination-in-chief. May I just remind you that you are still testifying pursuant to a solemn declaration that you made a few days ago, that you will be speaking the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. So please make yourself comfortable, and Mr. Jones can proceed with his examination.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, good afternoon, Mr. Buric.

utterances.speaker: Nesib Buric [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Before I resume, I just want to clarify two matters from your evidence last week. The first is, last Thursday you described how a delegation of the municipality of Srebrenica had gone through Ruljevici and seen the camp there in early 1992. I'm sure you recall giving that evidence. I simply, for the record, want you to tell us again who the president of Srebrenica municipality was, his name. Because it's even in the corrected transcript, it hasn't come out. So his name, please.

utterances.speaker: Nesib Buric [Resumed]
utterances.text: The president was Besim Ibisevic. And as to the delegation that when to Lijesce and came back to Boljevici, there was Becirevic, Hasan.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. And that helps. We have his surname, and believe it's Besim Ibisevic, starting with an I.

utterances.speaker: Nesib Buric [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Ibisevic, and his first name is Besim.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. On Friday you gave evidence about Kravica and the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. action in Kravica on the 7th of January, 1993. You gave a lot of evidence about weapons and ammunition which were captured. I just want to ask you this: Have you heard of a raketa, or rocket? Do you know what that refers to?

utterances.speaker: Nesib Buric [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never heard of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: What I mean firstly is have you actually heard of the weapon itself, never mind in relation to Kravica, a rocket, or raketa?

utterances.speaker: Nesib Buric [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I've never heard of it

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: In relation to Kravica, did you hear of a rocket or raketa being captured?

utterances.speaker: Nesib Buric [Resumed]
utterances.text: Definitely not.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And did you discuss amongst you, you who had been in Kravica, what had been captured? Is that something which was discussed amongst you?

utterances.speaker: Nesib Buric [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We collected the arms, and I said Zis was with me, and we gave most of those weapons to Glogova, and he took the weapons to Biljeg.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Okay. That's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, with the usher's assistance, I'd like to move on to the next exhibit on our list. It's D577. It might not be the next one on the list.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Mr. Buric, I'm going to ask you just to have a look at that document. It's a shortish one. I'm going to start by just reading a few sections from the document. Firstly, it's from the War Presidency of Srebrenica municipality. It's dated 23 January, 1993, and it's a report. The first paragraph I'm going to read into the record: "There is no peace in the area of Srebrenica today. From Zvijezda near Bratunac, the aggressor bombed the area of Potocari from a Howitzer practically the whole day and they fired at the town centre of Srebrenica from a VBR, multi-barelled missile launcher, from Nemici in Serbia. This artillery was followed by shots from anti-aircraft machine-guns and anti-aircraft cannons from Zvijezda and Kaolin, near Bratunac." The next paragraph: "The area of Osat and Kragljivoda and the newly liberated area of Jezero were targets for projectiles launched from VBR cannons and mortars." And then I'm moving down a bit further. I just want to read two other sentences into the record and then ask you some confession. The third paragraph: "14 persons in the territory of Srebrenica died of starvation, cold weather, and disease, including eight children below the age of 14. Forest fires were caused by aviation activities, with napalm bombs and incendiary shells in four locations, destroying the wood resources in this area. The aggressor fires at these areas from heavy artillery on a daily basis, which makes it more difficult for fire brigade teams to approach and put out the fires." There are a number of items mentioned here and I won't go into all of them. I specifically want to ask you about the reference to napalm bombs and ask whether during the war you ever came across the use by the Serbs of napalm.

utterances.speaker: Nesib Buric [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can state with a great deal of responsibility that I witnessed it myself. I think it was the 23rd of January, when the Serb forces shelled the area of Kusik [phoen] where I myself was, I couldn't believe what I saw. Basically snow was on fire. They were shelling us, and when the shells were landing and going off, there were some incendiary device inside and it would set the snow on fire. It was very cold. It was minus 20 degrees centigrade. And there was a metal pillar, and I could see that on fire. Had anybody told me this story, I would not have believed it. I saw it with my own eyes. There was this metal pillar that was on fire, as well as snow, and that was caused by those napalm shells that the Serbs were shelling us with.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Did you understand that to be some chemical which was burning on the snow? Do I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: Nesib Buric [Resumed]
utterances.text: When those shells would go off, we didn't actually know the nomenclature for that kind of weapon. We thought there was phosphorus inside, but I heard other people said that it was napalm and that it was much more contemporary, a much more modern kind of weapon used by the JNA

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Just one small matter, actually. The ELMO is between me and the witness. It's obscuring our view of each other. I'd just ask that it could be moved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Usher, please. I think if you- exactly- turn it and push it a little bit towards the back, it will be much better. I think it can still be reached by the witness. Is it okay now for you, Mr. Jones?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. There was a bit of hide-and-seek there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You should have told me before and I would have looked into it straight away. I didn't realise it myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'm not going to dwell, Mr. Buric, over-long on this document and on the situation in Srebrenica. Can I just ask you this: As referred to in this document, death from starvation, cold weather, and disease, was that common or uncommon in this period of January to March 1993?

utterances.speaker: Nesib Buric [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the medical files of Srebrenica, as far as I can remember, this is stated quite clearly. I think 60 people died of hunger in Srebrenica, and you can see it in the medical files. And that was a document drawn up by the doctors who used to work at Srebrenica. So that many people actually did die of hunger.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, moving on chronologically and turning to demilitarisation, what did you do following the demilitarisation of Srebrenica? I'm just -- that may be a very open question. Simply, what was your task, if any, in the period following demilitarisation?

utterances.speaker: Nesib Buric [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the fall of my village of Osmace on the 23rd of March, 1993, I withdrew to Srebrenica. And after the demilitarisation on the 18th of April, or to be more accurate, as of the 1st of May, I started working at the municipality of Srebrenica, and I was in charge of education, physical education, and sports, at the office of municipal councillor Avdic Hajrudin. And not much later, there was a new councilor, Fahrudin Salihovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: From the start of hostilities in 1992 to demilitarisation, did you in Osmace keep lists or anything of that description of the fighters in Osmace? Is that something which you maintained?

utterances.speaker: Nesib Buric [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never. Definitely not. For as long as I was in the area, up until the 1st of May, 1993, I can tell you that not a single paper of that sort existed with regard to the Osmace group.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Okay. Now, on Friday you told us at one point that you were taken prisoner subsequently by the Serbs, and a man called Petko from Obarak, I think it was, boasted that he took two Muslim civilians prisoner, Hajro and Osman. Just for the reference, this is page 4, lines 12 to 20, from Friday's LiveNote transcript. And that Hajro and Osman were still missing. Can you give us the name of that person again, please, his full name, if you know it, Petko.

utterances.speaker: Nesib Buric [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not captured by Petko. I don't know what is indicated in the documents. But I was injured on the 6th of July, 1995, and I sustained serious injuries, and there was the Dutch Battalion at the Srebrenica hospital, and we were handed over to the Serbs in Bratunac. And the person who was on call there, who was called Petko, who used to live in the house owned by Hasan Smajlovic, he told us, not to just me, there was about 150 of us - I can't remember correctly - that he had killed Hajro and Osman and that he captured Bahra, who was the daughter of Mahmut. I did not know any of these people in person, but I do remember that statement of his.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right. Now, do you know Petko's last name, or did you learn it at any stage?

utterances.speaker: Nesib Buric [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think Petrovic, but I know exactly where he used to live. There was a well-respected Muslim from Bratunac, Smajlovic Hasan, who is a veterinary surgeon, and he was a well-respected citizen of Bratunac and he lived in his house throughout the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And when Petko boasted that he had - just reading from the transcript - that he had killed Hajro and Osman and he captured Bahra, what period of time does this relate to?

utterances.speaker: Nesib Buric [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it must have been in May, June 1992, thereabouts, the capture of Bahra. In May or June 1992, but at any rate the first half of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And do you know in what area they were captured?

utterances.speaker: Nesib Buric [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the area of Poznanovici, just below the village of Poznanovici. Hajro and Osman were doing some work and he approached them and he captured them. And as to Bahra, she was captured in the course of the attack on the Muslim village of Joseva when it was on fire, the first time they tried to attack it was in May or June, as far as I can remember, 1992. So let me just make it clear. They used to burst into the areas, the Serbs from the neighbouring villages used to come to the village of Joseva and they would set a house or two alight. And they would push them back. But I think it was in May or June 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right. And from anything which Petko said, were you able to ascertain where he had come from in that time, where he was based in this time, in May, June 1992?

utterances.speaker: Nesib Buric [Resumed]
utterances.text: He told us to -- all of us, not just myself, as far as I can remember, there were three or four rooms there, full of injured people, and he was on call there. He was on duty. And he told us -- I think his village was Mlecva or Obarak since it is a small village, a hamlet, two or three houses. And they withdrew to Fakovici. That's where the battalion was. And he was a member of that battalion of theirs, the battalion of the Serb armed forces there. And he was there throughout the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So you've told us he was a member of that battalion that you've said was in Fakovici. Do you know whether or not he was in Fakovici on the 5th of October 1992?

utterances.speaker: Nesib Buric [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He approached me personally when I was on the stretcher and he indicated me and he said I -- he pointed a finger at me, in fact, and said to me: "I could have killed you at Fakovici when you took that three-barrelled gun and I didn't kill you because otherwise I wouldn't have been able to get out myself." "I was together with another guy from my unit hiding in the bushes. I had the machine-gun, 84-millimetre calibre, the one that you normally called 'death sower,' and I didn't kill you anyway. We just waited for the night to fall behind those bushes and we got out across the River Drina and crossed over into Serbia."

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So that's what he told you, and this is in July 1995; correct?

utterances.speaker: Nesib Buric [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, in July 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And just -- just out of interest, really: Did all of you wounded who were turned over by DutchBat to the Serbs, did you all survive?

utterances.speaker: Nesib Buric [Resumed]
utterances.text: After Sefik's death, the other tragedy that I'll never be able to forget is the fall of Srebrenica and the capture of the entire hospital in Srebrenica. There were about 200 wounded in Srebrenica. And on that day, on the 11th, when Srebrenica fell, some friends just carried us outside, and everything was left behind. And Serbs were already entering the town, and there was shooting around the hospital. They were shelling the post Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. office. I don't know. And we had three or four lorries, and we were taken to the accumulator, the akumulatori, and there were 200 of us. And then we were taken to Bratunac. And about 60 or 70 people who were only lightly wounded were taken away, and they went missing without any trace at all. I can give you the names of the wounded who were with me. I'm going to give you the list of people as far as I can remember. Semir Hrustic --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: For our purposes --

utterances.speaker: Nesib Buric [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me finish and then you can ask me the other questions. So about 60 people were killed. About 60 were taken to a camp at Batkovici, and those of us who were seriously wounded, 60 or 70, were taken to the Tuzla hospital. And it was on the 6th of July, after the fall of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I want to pass the next exhibit to the witness. It has ERN number 01320782. We have copies for distribution.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, this, as you can see, it's a list from December. The year isn't indicated, but we can perhaps get there. A list of soldiers from the 5th Battalion. It should say "for payment." For payment. And I just would ask you firstly to look at number 25 on this list. We see Petko Petrovic, number 25. Do you see that, Mr. Buric?

utterances.speaker: Nesib Buric [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You referred to a battalion in Fakovici in October 1992. Do you know if that was the 5th Battalion or do you or do you not know what it was called?

utterances.speaker: Nesib Buric [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what it was called. I can see number 25, Petko Petrovic. I don't know what it was called.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And as far as you know, that's the name of the man who had this conversation with you about his presence in Fakovici in October 1992?

utterances.speaker: Nesib Buric [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose that must be him.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'll ask for an exhibit number, please, for this document.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: D747, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So this document will become Defence Exhibit D747.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And the next exhibit is also new. It's 04337008.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And this document is dated 4th October 1992. I'll just read it for the record while the witness is given the document. Command of the Bratunac garrison, confidential number 243-9, 4 October 1992, to command of the Birac Brigade: "It is mainly ambush action that is being carried out in the area of responsibility of the 5th Battalion. On the night of 3, 4 October 1992, an ambush was set out in the sector of the Sase mine, Bojici [phoen]. Our group killed two enemy soldiers and wounded five or six of them who managed to run away. The bodies of enemy soldiers were pulled out, one Kalashnikov and two handmade pistols were captured."

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, this document is dated 4th of October, 1992, refers to the 5th Battalion. We saw reference in a document a moment ago to the 5th Battalion, with a Petko Petrovic in it. Now, the Birac Brigade, is that a brigade which you are familiar with? Does that name mean anything to you?

utterances.speaker: Nesib Buric [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know on the basis of history what Birac is. That's Srebrenica, Bratunac, and Vlasenica, which is a part of Zvornik which is covered by the region of Birac. So I suppose it must be a brigade, on the basis of such a name. Birac is a region.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. And you gave evidence a moment ago about how this Petrovic had captured people in, I think you said Poznanovici. Here there's a reference to an ambush in Sase, which is, again, some distance from Fakovici. My question is: Based on your experience and if you can help us with this, would it surprise you if a battalion from Fakovici were operating in Sase, Poznanovici, and in those areas?

utterances.speaker: Nesib Buric [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were active in that area, especially Muslims. Since there was this overall chaos and hunger, Muslims would go and get food in their villages, Voljavica and Sase. And they went on a daily basis, setting ambushes for those people who were going to collect food. For example, to get some corn from Voljevica and Zanjevo, and that was the area of operations of that battalion from Fakovici.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: All right. Okay. So the battalion from Fakovici was active in those areas which you've also mentioned, Voljevica, Sase, Zanjevo?

utterances.speaker: Nesib Buric [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Can I have a number for this document, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This document, Mr. Jones, will become Defence Exhibit D748.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, just a few more documents. If the witness could be shown Prosecution Exhibit P566, which is a book by Nijaz Masic, "Srebrenica: Aggression, Resistance, Treason, Genocide," published in 1999. I want to ask you, Mr. Buric, firstly, are you familiar with -- well, firstly, do you know Nijaz Masic?

utterances.speaker: Nesib Buric [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And are you familiar with this book?

utterances.speaker: Nesib Buric [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did hear that he wrote a book, but believe me, I didn't read any of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You say that with a slight smile. Is there any reason why you didn't read the book or any opinions you have about the book?

utterances.speaker: Nesib Buric [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what to say. I didn't read it. I really can't comment on that at all. I didn't read a word of it. And as far as Masic is concerned, he's a historian, and people who write history or about history, they lie a lot.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Well, let's -- firstly I want to go to page -- I think it's page 2 in the English. It says: "The list of the persons that assisted me in the technical and expert parts of my writing is too long. I express special gratitude to ..." And five lines down it says "Buric, Nesib." My first question is: Did you ever meet Nijaz Masic and consult with him on the writing of this book?

utterances.speaker: Nesib Buric [Resumed]
utterances.text: Masic came to me only one time, at the place where I worked. And as far as I can remember, he wanted some kind of financial assistance in order to print or to publish a book, and it was probably this book. This is what I can remember. He wanted for the association of military disabled veterans give him some kind of contribution in order to publish this book. That's where I was working at the time, and I think that, as far as I can remember, he came and he asked for some money.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Okay. So in that financial capacity, then, he approached you. Did you provide him information about Osmace and events in Osmace in 1992, 1993?

utterances.speaker: Nesib Buric [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: If we turn to the next page in English, we have a section, it's an extract, obviously, but on Osmace. And in the B/C/S it's going to be page 01099744. And in Bosnian, if you see Osmace and then you go down four paragraphs, there's a paragraph which in Bosnian starts [B/C/S spoken], 1992. Do you see that? I'll read it in English?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The usher would need to go down two further paragraphs, please. Yes. Go ahead, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: In English it says: "We could breathe easier when the Skelani unit led by Tihic was formed end of May 1992. This unit forms a guard on Biljeg facility, above the village of Miholjevine; then help to Poznanovici follows. The soldiers," in fact in Bosnian it's [B/C/S spoken], which we would say should be "fighters," but, "the soldiers or fighters from Osmace, Kragljivoda, Biljeg, Skenderovici, and Stari Grad, helped in the destruction" - and we've had the issue, and we say that's liquidation rather than destruction - "of the Chetnik strongholds in Ratkovici," and it mentions the hamlets. I simply want to ask you this: You told us last week that 20 or 50 men from Osmace - sorry - I'll read the quote. You said, and this is page 79, line 7 to 15 of Thursday's transcript. You said: "I can state with a great deal of responsibility that as far as my group of 20 or 50-something men from Osmace are concerned, nobody participated in any action in the area of Ratkovici." So my question is this: Looking at this section of the Masic book saying that soldiers from Osmace helped in the liquidation of Ratkovici, is that accurate or inaccurate?

utterances.speaker: Nesib Buric [Resumed]
utterances.text: I state with a great deal of certainty that Osmace was not -- there was nobody from Osmace in Ratkovici. There were no armed formations or groups in the events there. Nobody was even -- from Osmace was there anywhere near that date.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So as far as the book is concerned and what you read there, does that reflect the truth or not?

utterances.speaker: Nesib Buric [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is 100 per cent untrue.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honours, one matter. The same point arises in relation to P95, but rather than presenting P95 and asking for the same comment, I would just note for the record that it's page 12 of that exhibit, the same issue arises of fighters from Osmace participate in Ratkovici. So I'm not going to put that to the witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, thank you, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: -- just for expediency, I make that mention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I take it that that is acceptable with the Prosecution. Mr. Di Fazio?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I don't have P95. Can I get back to you on this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Certainly. But try to get back --

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes, immediately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- before he finishes his examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. It's page 12 of that exhibit. It's just that one point. Now, if the witness could be shown, yes, P90, Prosecution Exhibit P90, and this is the book, "Naser Oric, Srebrenica." And I'm going to start just by referring to page 2 in the English, which is in the foreword. So in B/C/S, it's page 5. Page 5. In the English it says: "I have not been able to collect all the data and research all the sources that would make this war complete, because the war is not yet -- not over yet and the evidence is still being gathered and classified. Anyway, it has not been my intention to make this the final work on the events past. On the contrary, I want to invite new discussions and new arguments so that we may get closer to the real truth." I want to ask about that in a second. It's the next page in English, the extract, page 89.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: If you can see, Mr. Buric, in the B/C/S, it's page 159 to 160. One moment, please. And it's the quote in English, page 89, sixth paragraph, last sentence, where it says: "The town of Srebrenica was fully opened towards the Kragljivoda area in June 1992, after the aggressor had been beaten in the fights for Jasenova, Turija, and Pribojevici." Now, Mr. Buric, you gave us evidence about the situation in Kragljivoda and Osmace in June 1992. Is that true, that sentence, that Srebrenica and Kragljivoda were fully opened up towards each other in June 1992?

utterances.speaker: Nesib Buric [Resumed]
utterances.text: In June 1992, they were not linked, because the Serb settlements of Postonje and Podrid were there. We also had Brezani, where their Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. communications where. There were also incursions by Serb units from Podravanje and Srpska Jasenova. I'm not sure exactly what the date was when the Serbs left Podravanje. They left and left the village behind. But definitely in June there was no contact, there was no free communication between Kragljivoda and Osmace.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You would disagree with what's written there as being accurate? All right. Sorry, the witness said "ne" a couple of times. It hasn't been interpreted. Is what you read in that book accurate or inaccurate?

utterances.speaker: Nesib Buric [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, I take it that you mean to say that it is not accurate.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm just interested in knowing the date. When did the Serbs withdraw from Brezani, if you can help?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'm afraid I can't help with that, Mr. Buric. It's your evidence.

utterances.speaker: Nesib Buric [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that this was in late May, and I state certainly that the Serbs withdrew on the 30th of June. So at this time, there was no communication between these two places. When the Serbs withdrew from Brezani towards Podravanje and came from Postolje and Podrid, then there was some kind of communication between the two places. But this was already most probably beginning of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. That's clear. We saw in the preface some remarks about the circumstances under which this book was written. Do you know anything about this book purportedly by Naser Oric, how it was written or with or by whom?

utterances.speaker: Nesib Buric [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that this book was also written by Nijaz Masic. The war was still going on in Bosnia. I was clear earlier. Those who write history also lie a lot.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Okay. There are historians who might take exception to that, but we'll take that point, and will show, if we may, an extract from P328, which is a segment of an interview. And the reference to the transcript is tape 3, side A, pages 8 to 10. We need to obviously have the sound. I don't know if that involves the technical booth making a switch.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What I noticed was that the tape was running, but there was no sound.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Okay. We'll run it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: SPEAKER: I just want to talk about this book that I wrote and in particular I want to talk about how this book came to be. With the very demilitarisation of Srebrenica, when the UN came into Srebrenica, we then stopped our military activities, and our whole military ...

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honours, I in fact wanted to just play a small extract of this exhibit. However, I'm just thinking again now that in fact, given the answers which this witness has given, it suffices really to draw Your Honours' attention to this exhibit and to the particular portion. And rather than playing it, which might be a bit long-winded, I can simply read this section that I'm interested in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I think it will be quicker. And it's the section where Naser Oric, I think I can lead to that, the speaker says: "So the manuscript was finished within 15 days. The whole thing went up to Sweden. And then from Sweden to Ljubljana, and then it was printed. To tell you the truth, I haven't even managed to read it." Further down: "So if they lied about me in the book or exaggerated the things that were happening, because you know how it goes, people exaggerate things a little bit to make their own role seem larger than it really is. They exaggerated my role most of all."

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Buric, you mentioned that historians, as you say, lie sometimes, or a lot. Specifically, as far as Mr. Masic is concerned, do you have any comment to make about this -- this extract which we've just read out from the interview about exaggerations of the roles played by Naser Oric?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: If Your Honours please, has the witness testified he's even read this? How can he answer such a question? I mean ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The witness hasn't been asked the question as yet, whether he's read the book.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: No, but he's been invited to comment on the content of the book and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He's also told it was written by Masic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: That's his evidence. That was absolutely his evidence. He said this book was written by Masic, and so it was really a question of whether Masic was reliable --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He didn't say that it was definitely written by Masic. He said there is suspicion, sort of, that it was written by Masic and not by Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: He said: "I think that this book was also written by Nijaz Masic"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But "I think" is "I think." He's not sure about it. If he's sure about it, he better tell us that he knows for sure that it was written by --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Mr. Buric, how confident are you in that opinion that the book was written by Nijaz Masic, the Oric book?

utterances.speaker: Nesib Buric [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume, but I'm not sure, I assume that this book was written by Nijaz Masic too.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Why do you make that assumption?

utterances.speaker: Nesib Buric [Resumed]
utterances.text: While I was working at the municipal office, there were two or three historians there. I think the only person who came from Srebrenica was Nijaz Masic, so I assume that that is his book and that his influence in the book was as much as 99 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: All right. Well, I'll move on from that exhibit and that subject. I think that's sufficient. Finally, three more exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, because I think we need to clear this. Are you pursuing the question that Mr. Di Fazio sort of objected to or not? Or are you dropping it?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Well, I'll ask this witness if he's read the book. I can pursue it to that extent. I'm satisfied with his answer, considering the likelihood it was written by Masic, and his opinion of the Masic book.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: All right. I'd ask if the witness could be shown P9. I'm not going to put that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Just a quick question on this document, Mr. Buric. This is staff of the Srebrenica armed forces, purportedly, dated 15 October 1992. It's allegedly an order of the OVH staff to form brigades. You've told us already that there wasn't a battalion in Osmace in 1992, so I'm not going to ask you about that. It's the items which appear on page 2 of the English and also page 2 of Bosnian, or the bottom of page 1, where it says: "Formation of the following independent branch and service units." And we see mortar company, in English it has mortar, COY, but [B/C/S spoken]. Are you aware of whether there was ever a mortar company formed in Srebrenica. Sorry, not ever; before demilitarisation.

utterances.speaker: Nesib Buric [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not aware of that. And I believe that there probably wasn't a mortar company there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And how about the next item, an armoured platoon?

utterances.speaker: Nesib Buric [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know if they're thinking of horses being in some platoon, but there was no armoured platoon. There was no armoured equipment in Srebrenica. So why would an armoured platoon be there?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. That's all I want to ask on this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, if the witness could be shown D561. And this purports to be a list of information on combat operations from an attack on Gradina, from the 2nd of June, 1992. Now, firstly, I want to take - and I think we need the last page in Bosnian on the ELMO, please. I want to take -- draw your attention to the second name on the right-hand side, where in English we have -- first we have source information, Mirsad Dudic, and in the English it says Nesib Buric. Is that what you read in a Bosnian, the number 2, or do you read something else? It's further down, under [B/C/S spoken]. Yes, number 2. Can you read what it says there, please, Mr. Buric, in number 2.

utterances.speaker: Nesib Buric [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nesib Buric, commander of the Osmace TO platoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, do you know anyone of that name in Osmace who might be described as having any commanding role in Osmace, or does that refer to you?

utterances.speaker: Nesib Buric [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is supposed to be me here, but I had no platoon. I was no commander, not a commander of a platoon. Like I said, I had about ten men in my group. This was like my family, those who were with me. There was no platoon. The entire Osmace --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: That's fine. I want to establish this: Is that actually your signature?

utterances.speaker: Nesib Buric [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. This is definitely not my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: How in fact do you sign your name? I'm not asking you to give a demonstration, but do you write "Nesib Buric" or "Buric, Nesib," or what precisely do you write when you sign?

utterances.speaker: Nesib Buric [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's very short. I never use my full signature, very rarely on a document. My signature is completely different.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Were you a source of information for this combat sheet, this combat action sheet? Did you provide information to the 2nd Corps or to anyone about this action?

utterances.speaker: Nesib Buric [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 1st of May, 1993, when I started to work at the Srebrenica municipal office, I had never even glanced into any kind of military office or institution. The only time would be if I personally needed some kind of paper or certificate or something. So I never stepped into any kind of military office until the 1st of May, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: All right. First of all, did you either fill in this form? Firstly, I'll ask you that. Did you fill in this form?

utterances.speaker: Nesib Buric [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the first time that I'm seeing this.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And did you ever go to Zivinice, in 1997, specifically?

utterances.speaker: Nesib Buric [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And just a couple of questions on the information in this document. Was Bektic, Nedzad, Nedzad Bektic, was he a commander of the 3rd of May Brigade on the 2nd of June, 1992?

utterances.speaker: Nesib Buric [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that there was no brigade at all. He had his own group, Karacici, so he was in Karacici the entire time.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right. So I take it the answer is no. Mirsad Dudic, was he the commander of Osmace TO.

utterances.speaker: Nesib Buric [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. Mirsad Dudic was not a commander. He had a group of about ten men. In my village, he was together with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. We all heard it the, no, no was answering my question, so I take it the answer was no, the witness answered, and then the next --

utterances.speaker: Nesib Buric [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right. Thank you. So in your opinion is the information which Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. you can see on this document, is it reliable? Is it accurate?

utterances.speaker: Nesib Buric [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is 100 per cent untrue, and I don't know where these papers were filled in.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And we have a similar document, P87. If that can be shown to the witness. It's the final document. I'll be finished very shortly. And just for the record, this deals with an alleged attack on Ducici on the 19th of June, 1992. And again, if you could first look at the last page and tell us whether that's meant to be your name and whether that's your signature.

utterances.speaker: Nesib Buric [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not my signature. It states "Nesib Buric, commander of the Osmace TO platoon." But somebody else filled this in. I don't know where this comes from. This is not my signature. I state definitely that I never saw Ducici in my life, and I never went to Ducici either.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And as far as you know, was Osmace TO commanded by Atif Krdzic, the unit in charge of combat operations in Ducici on the 19th of June, 1992?

utterances.speaker: Nesib Buric [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me. Could you repeat the name, please. I didn't understand it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Atif Krdzic.

utterances.speaker: Nesib Buric [Resumed]
utterances.text: Atif Krdzic was in our group at Osmace. And as I said, not a single man from Osmace went to the territory of Ratkovici.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So finally, if you could look at paragraphs 2, 3, 4, and 5 of this document, which purports to set out the units which were involved in this action and tell us whether, as far as you know, this is accurate, reliable information or not.

utterances.speaker: Nesib Buric [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't go to that area, so I don't know which groups were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Okay. Let me ask you just one final question, then. You see paragraph 5, we see the name Zurijet Mujic. Do you know Zurijet Mujic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Muhic or Mujic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Zurijet Mujic is -- I'm familiar with him. I know his name. I didn't have any contacts with him. He couldn't have been in that area. Zurijet is part of the Skenderovici area. Actually, I know him personally and I believe that he could not have been physically present in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. My apologies. It was Mujic. And where was he from, Zurijet Mujic?

utterances.speaker: Nesib Buric [Resumed]
utterances.text: Zurijet Mujic is from Skenderovici. It says Srebrenica here, but it's not, actually. He's have Skenderovici.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Okay. Just finally, when did you leave the army, the Bosnian army?

utterances.speaker: Nesib Buric [Resumed]
utterances.text: On May 1st, when I started to work at the Srebrenica municipal office, in 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And did you have any contact with the 28th Division of the army after demilitarisation, or after your retirement?

utterances.speaker: Nesib Buric [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And did you have any role in this project of preparing these information sheets on actions?

utterances.speaker: Nesib Buric [Resumed]
utterances.text: In March 1992, from March 1992 until 1995, until I was wounded, I did not write a single paper or no single document or piece of paper was issued from the -- or by the Osmace group.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Jones. Mr. Buric, we are going to move to the cross-examination, which will be conducted by Mr. Di Fazio. I just remind you of what I advised you the first day when you arrived in this courtroom, namely, that you have the same obligations to answer the questions fully and truthfully, irrespective of who is putting the question to you. So the same obligation applies also when the questions are being put by the officer of the Prosecution. Mr. Di Fazio.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honours. Just give me a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Mr. Buric, my name is Mr. Di Fazio. I have some questions for you. Moments ago, you were asked by Mr. Jones: "Just finally, when did you leave the army, the Bosnian army?" And you said: "On May 1st, when I started work at the Srebrenica municipal office in 1993." What was your role in the Bosnian army that you had prior to May 1st 1993? What rank did you hold in it?

utterances.speaker: Nesib Buric [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had no rank whatsoever. I never got a rank.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: All right. But you were in the army. Were you a private? You've just told us. You just told us that you left the army and then went to work in Srebrenica in May 1st, 1993. So what rank did you hold, what position did you hold in the Bosnian army prior to May of 1993?

utterances.speaker: Nesib Buric [Resumed]
utterances.text: I made myself clear. There was no official army. There were armed groups. And I had about ten people with me in my village, Mahala, in Osmace. As I said, ten people were with me. Five or six out of them were actually armed. So that group of about ten people was where I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I see. So it was just a failure on your part to correct Mr. Jones, and say, "Well, actually, Mr. Jones, there was no army in Bosnia prior to May in the Srebrenica area, prior to May of 1993." Is that what you really meant to say?

utterances.speaker: Nesib Buric [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I said that there were armed groups.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: But no Bosnian army structure in existence of any sort or description whatsoever in 1992 and the first few months of 1993? That's your position, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: Nesib Buric [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is. With regard to my group, for instance, nobody gave us any rifles. Nobody allocated any logistics or barracks or anything to us. Already in the introductory part of my evidence, I said that it was just a resistance on the part of the population, in order for them not to be destroyed, as has been the case in some other villages, for example, as it happened in May and June 1992 and until 1993. We got organised amongst ourselves within the village to defend the village. So I can state with a great deal of responsibility that we were not given rifles, uniforms, or any logistical support from anyone whosoever. And it was just an armed resistance on the part of the population.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay, well, we'll return to this topic later. Mr. Nijaz Masic. You say he's a historian. And do you also say that he is a man who is given to lying when he writes? Is this -- I want to be clear about your evidence. Do I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: Nesib Buric [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do apologise. I have to say something quite apart from this courtroom. A well-known writer in Bosnia, Ivo Andric, in one of his books, The Travnik Chronicles, said "it is not he who doesn't know how to read who is stupid." The ones who believe that whatever has been written is true are even more stupid. So that's the essence of my comment. In those areas, the former Yugoslavia, Bosnia and Herzegovina, I didn't mean the world as a whole. But in my part of the world, history tends to be misrepresented, and, for example, the battle of Kosovo, even though it had been lost, it somehow turned out to have been won. It is just by way of example. I wasn't going to actually quote this example now.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: So is it your position that what Mr. Nijaz Masic writes in his books is unreliable because historians in your part of the world are unreliable? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: Nesib Buric [Resumed]
utterances.text: Facts tend to be blown out of all proportion, things are exaggerated a million times. And that's why this is written in that way. I mean, I haven't read the book, but even the small passage that refers to Osmace is definitely not true, and on the basis of that, I believe that 99 per cent of the book isn't true.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: So the Trial Chamber can understand your evidence very clearly. You haven't read this book, you don't know what's in it, apart from what's been pointed out to you this afternoon by Mr. Jones, but you can quite confidently say that the rest is rubbish; is that correct, not having read it, not having read it?

utterances.speaker: Nesib Buric [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I was referring to the passage that was read out to me. I didn't read the book by either Naser or by Masic, but I can definitely state, confidently state, that what was read out to me in relation to Osmace is a lie.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: How does that lead you to conclude, if you do, that the rest -- the remainder of the book is either -- contains untruths or is not credible?

utterances.speaker: Nesib Buric [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't actually say anything about the rest of the book. I said I didn't know what was included in the rest of the book. I referred to the passage that was read out to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Look, isn't it the case that your evidence just -- just moments ago, a few moments ago as Defence counsel was finishing his cross-examination, your evidence regarding this book was that Mr. Nijaz Masic was a historian and was quite possibly given to lying? That's the impression you wanted to convey to the Trial Chamber; isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: Nesib Buric [Resumed]
utterances.text: The part that I did read, of course. Only that bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I see. Now, Mr. Nijaz Masic, you had some dealings with him after demilitarisation. Was that in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: Nesib Buric [Resumed]
utterances.text: I worked at the municipality as a person in charge of education, culture, and sports, and Masic was a teacher of history at the school there, and that's how I knew him.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Did you know that he was writing a book, a history or a -- an account of events in Srebrenica in -- at least in the period 1992/1993? Did you know that?

utterances.speaker: Nesib Buric [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know that. No, I didn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Do I understand your evidence to be that he approached you, or the organisation you worked with, with a view to obtaining funding for his book?

utterances.speaker: Nesib Buric [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: The result was you refused him, or your organisation did? I don't mean that in any bad way, but you said: "No, we don't have any money available for you. We can't fund you"?

utterances.speaker: Nesib Buric [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember. I think he did get some money, but I can't remember how much. I think a very small amount, 100 or 200 Deutschmarks, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Were you instrumental at all in arranging for that 100 or 200 Deutschmarks to be given to him? Did you play a part in that decision?

utterances.speaker: Nesib Buric [Resumed]
utterances.text: The main role was played by the chief of the municipality. I was his assistant. And there was simply a request that I saw and I processed, but I did not play any role in terms of suggesting anything at the municipality. Councilor was Fahrudin Salilovic or maybe somebody called Markic. I can't remember. At any rate, it is the councilor's office that decided what was to be done.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: So Mr. -- sorry - Mr. Nijaz Masic would have no particular reason to be grateful to you for any assistance in the creation or the writing, publication, of his book?

utterances.speaker: Nesib Buric [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe one thing: I don't think it was about providing assistance or not providing assistance. But since I was involved with education, culture, and sports, he hugged me from that point of view, rather than in terms of some kind of payment. He thought that it was good form to include my name as well. I think he also thanked a dead man, Alic Zajko. I don't know why he would want to thank a dead man. He was killed Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. during the attack on Srebrenica, and he nevertheless includes him in the list of acknowledgments.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: How do you know that he thought it was good form to include your name in the list of contributors to his book?

utterances.speaker: Nesib Buric [Resumed]
utterances.text: You'd have to ask him. I don't know, believe me.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: No. I'm asking you, because you said it. You said just now that he thought it would be good form to include you in his book. But your evidence is that you had done very, very little to assist him in getting the book published. So why do you say that he thought it would be good form to help you, to acknowledge your contribution?

utterances.speaker: Nesib Buric [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was quite clear in what I said. I said that organising any sort of education in Srebrenica, to collect children from the streets, it was a huge effort. And we're talking about 7.000 students besieged by poverty, hunger, and everything else. And we nevertheless managed to organise something to take care of those children, and I was involved in that. And I believe that's why he thought he should mention my name.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Let's turn to another book, Exhibit P -- actually, on reflection, no. Let's just stay with this current topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Can the witness be shown P566, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Let's have a look at the contributors to the book. Your name is included. Your attention has already been drawn to your name. I think if you scroll down through the names that are listed there, you'll come across the name of Mr. Naser Oric. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: Nesib Buric [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Do you have any idea what contribution, if any, Mr. Oric made to this book?

utterances.speaker: Nesib Buric [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Are you in a position to say that he made no contribution to the book?

utterances.speaker: Nesib Buric [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that 60 per cent of these names are names of people who made no contribution whatsoever. I don't know for what reason they are listed here and I don't know for what reason Naser Oric's name is listed here.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Just explain that last answer that you gave to the Trial Chamber. Just explain to the Trial Chamber on what basis you believe that 60 per cent of the names that are written in this particular document are the names of people who made no contribution whatsoever. What is the basis for that assertion?

utterances.speaker: Nesib Buric [Resumed]
utterances.text: Alija Zilic [phoen] - okay. He was never in Srebrenica. Zulik Fikar [phoen], Hasic, Amir [phoen] was never in Srebrenica either. Abdurahman Sarajlic was never there, Nermina Sacic. And these names just caught my eye. And I really don't see on what basis these names would be listed here, in much the same way as my name and Naser's name. Either Catic, Smajl [phoen], Cekic, they were never present in the area of Srebrenica. They did nothing there. Nizama Delkic and Dizdarevic seems to be -- no. Begic Sabit. There was nothing they could have provided him with, no data. I don't know why he's thanking them, but I just looked at this list briefly and I spotted quite a few names of people who had nothing whatsoever to do with Srebrenica. And some of these people are dead, Zali Cajko [phoen] is a dead man.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Do you say that those people were never in Srebrenica, do you mean that they were never in the Srebrenica area, for example, they are from Croatia or perhaps Germany or somewhere else? Or they weren't in Srebrenica town itself?

utterances.speaker: Nesib Buric [Resumed]
utterances.text: They're not originally from that area and they were not in Srebrenica. They were somewhere else. And originally, they came from other parts of the country.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay. Now, Mr. Nijaz Masic has written in his book, this little portion that deals with Osmace and that Defence counsel showed you, and you know that's the next page in the exhibit. And we've heard your evidence that it's just nonsense, what's written there, it's not true at all. Would you agree with me in this sense: You are a person who could really provide good information about events in Osmace? Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: Nesib Buric [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can give you 100 per cent information with regard to Osmace.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. And would you agree that if Mr. Masic were to set about writing a book and include in it a chapter about Osmace, you would be a good person to go and speak to in order to get that information? You'd have to agree with that, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: Nesib Buric [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't give him any information and I don't believe anyone else from Osmace would provide any information, and I believe that whatever he has written came from his own head. And I can say that Masic was certainly not in the area of Osmace during the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I understand that. All I'm saying to you is this: A person in Mr. Masic's position, wanting to write a book about events in Srebrenica in 1992, and perhaps early 1993, and who wanted to include a section dealing with events in Osmace, you, and perhaps many other men, but you, certainly, would be in a good position to help him out? You agree with that, don't you?

utterances.speaker: Nesib Buric [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do have the information, but I wouldn't have provided Masic with that information. I'm sorry, but, no, I wouldn't provide him with the information.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I just want to be clear about that. You say "wouldn't." Do I understand you to be saying that you would not like to, you would not consider doing it, or is it the case that you are simply saying that you did not, in fact, provide him with information about Osmace?

utterances.speaker: Nesib Buric [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can state with a great deal of responsibility that I never provided any information, and I never heard of anyone else from Osmace providing any information either. I don't know what his sources were. But definitely I myself did not breathe a word to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I've finished with that exhibit for the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: You were also shown Exhibit P90, which is purportedly, on the face of it, a book written by Mr. Oric. And you said that you think that this book was written by Mr. Nijaz Masic, when you were shown it. And you also said that you assume the book was written by Mr. Nijaz Masic. Now, why do you make that assumption?

utterances.speaker: Nesib Buric [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. It just came to mind. I suppose it could have been written by Nijaz Masic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Mr. Buric, you're testifying in a war crimes trial. You undertake -- you understand your responsibility here is an extremely serious one, don't you?

utterances.speaker: Nesib Buric [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes. And you can understand, can't you, that the credibility - sorry. I withdraw that. The authorship of a book written by the accused in this trial is a matter that might concern the Trial Chamber? You understand that, the true authorship of the book?

utterances.speaker: Nesib Buric [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do understand that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Jones. One moment, Mr. Di Fazio.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Simply this. I don't think it's appropriate for my learned friend to remind the witness of this point of the solemn obligation, et cetera, when the question about why did you make that assumption was put in precise terms by me and the witness answered it. He's been asked again. If the witness is somewhat nonplussed being asked it a second time, I don't think it's the occasion to start lecturing him about the solemnity of his task. The question was asked. It may be unclear why it's being asked again. And the reference is page 24, line 11: "Why do you make that assumption?" Absolutely the same question Mr. Di Fazio's put, and he gave an answer. Now, if Mr. Di Fazio isn't happy with the answer the witness gave, that's more a matter for him than for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Di Fazio. Because he -- indeed he did -- Mr. Jones did put that question and you actually repeated the same question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes, but the witness has now said it just came to mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: That's what I'm concerned about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The only innovation and novelty is in the way he has answered the question. I agree with you that perhaps it wasn't a case of putting the same question again, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Well, I'm only interested in this answer: "It came to mind." That's all I'm interested in.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And, Witness, I'm certainly not intending to lecture you. I don't want you to feel intimidated in any way. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: Nesib Buric [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not at all intimidated.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Good.

utterances.speaker: Nesib Buric [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I may, I would just like to point out that I am unable to comment on books which I haven't even set eyes on, let alone read. So I can't really comment on something that I have no idea about.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Well, that's precisely my point, Mr. Buric. You see, you were asked on what basis did you assume that Nijaz Masic wrote P90, the book that's apparently, on the face of it, written by Naser Oric, and you've just told us: "Well, it just came to mind." Why did you tell the Trial Chamber that you assumed it was written by Mr. Nijaz Masic when it just came to your mind? Why didn't you stop and think: Well, actually, I don't have any information about who wrote the book, and I'll tell the Trial Chamber that? Is there any reason why you didn't provide that answer instead?

utterances.speaker: Nesib Buric [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because I wasn't commenting on the actual contents of the book. I couldn't have done that. And there were one, two, three, four, five, ten questions. And I didn't even try to comment on the contents of the book. And then it simply crossed my mind, but I really am unable to comment, because I don't know who could have written it, because this is the first time that I'm seeing this book.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I don't think I need to show you the book. If you want to see it, by all means.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: But the front of the book, first page, I suppose, the beginning of the book, let's call it the beginning of the book, says: "Naser Oric, Srebrenica, testifies and an -- and accuses genocide of Bosniaks in East Bosnia, April 1992 to September 1994." And he then -- then there's a foreword, and at the bottom of it, Naser Oric, the name Naser Oric, appears. Is there anything that you can think of or anything that you're aware of, I should say, that makes you think that Naser Oric did not author the book, as appears to be the case on the face of it? We know now that it's got nothing to do with Nijaz Masic, because that just came to mind, so is there any other reason that you say that this book is not what it appears to be, a book written by a man named Naser Oric?

utterances.speaker: Nesib Buric [Resumed]
utterances.text: In order to write a book, I mean, I'm a mathematician by profession, so in order to write about it I need to know the matter, to be very familiar with it. And if I were to write a book, I would write about my Osmace. I wouldn't write about anything else. I couldn't describe or write about anything that I didn't see for myself. So I assume, in order Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. to do something properly, Naser had to have been there, to have seen it in order to write about it. I don't see any other reason. I could write and talk about my Osmace, but couldn't talk about any other place because I couldn't comment or talk about or write about anything that I myself didn't see.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I just want to show you a clip of a group of people in a room talking.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Would Your Honours just give me a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, certainly, Mr. Di Fazio.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "This question was unclear to me, this question and the other question."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, we have it now. Perhaps you could start again, Mr. Di Fazio, please. We are at 14:41:50, point 08. That's what we have on the screen. On the clock, actually, itself, which is the bottom of the picture, above the script. On the right-hand side, it says "02 hours, 27 minutes, point seventeen, two." That's where we are.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: It's only a very, very brief, extremely brief passage.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "This question was unclear to me, this one and the other question. I was confused about this the whole time, so I called Masic again, as he was the man who heard the history of what happened in that part of the world and of these events, and so he has quite a lot of material and also knows the most about what actually happened. So he wrote quite a lot of notes and so on."

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Now, I just have one question. You can see this table -- in what's depicted on the screen, you can see the table, papers on it, and a number of men, and at the very end of the table, a gentleman there, longish hair, shoulder-length hair. Do you recognise that man? If I suggested --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't understand whether the witness said yes or no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I heard the witness say "ne."

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: If I suggested to you that was plainly Mr. Oric --

utterances.speaker: Nesib Buric [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see anything on the monitor. I have just -- I can see a door.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: That explains your answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Can you see now on the monitor anything, Mr. Buric, or what are you seeing now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's clearer now. I can see Naser Oric in front.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes. When you say "in front," just to be absolutely clear, as you look at the image --

utterances.speaker: Nesib Buric [Resumed]
utterances.text: He's sitting in the middle, next to the door or in front of the door. That's where I see Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Fine. Thank you. Now, the rest of -- you heard the clip, and Mr. Oric seems to be talking about Mr. Masic in a manner, I suggest, that indicates he's got confidence in him as a man you can deal with in terms of events in 1992, reporting and discussing events in 1992. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: Nesib Buric [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never saw Naser or Masic in 1993. The first time I saw Naser was - I don't know - sometime in late March or early April of 1993. The first time I saw Masic was in May 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: That might be so. I'm not actually asking that. In fact, I think that if you look on the screen, you'll see that these -- what's happening there has occurred years later. But what I'm interested in is what Mr. Oric has to say about Nijaz Masic. He seems to take the view that he's a man who can be approached with regard to obtaining of information about events in 1992. That's what I suggest to you Mr. Oric is saying. Don't you agree?

utterances.speaker: Nesib Buric [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what their connection was. My personal opinion is that if anyone were to write or go about writing a good-quality book, they wouldn't allow Masic to write it. And I can explain why I believe this, but at a closed session, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
