utterances.text: Would you say that if someone was going to write a book about events in 1992, that Mr. Naser Oric would be in a good position to write such a book, that he would have access to the sort of information that would permit him to write an authoritative book?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I realise Mr. Di Fazio is perhaps moving away from an explanation which this witness is going to give, but, clearly, if the witness wants to explain in more detail in private session, then of course he shouldn't be forced to do it in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm coming to that. But let him answer the question first. The question that Mr. Di Fazio requires you to answer is the following, Mr. Buric: Would you say that if someone was going to write a book about events in 1992, that Mr. Naser Oric would be in a good position to write such a book, that he would have access to the sort of information that would permit him to write an authoritative book? Would you agree with that statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wouldn't agree, and I believe 99 per cent, with 99 per cent certainty, that Naser did not have even 80 per cent of the information about what was going on in the Srebrenica region. All the events that were talked about later, exaggerated, I don't know, that's something that happened. And I believe that Naser did not have the right or the proper information about what was happening in the territory of the Srebrenica region.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Now let's go into private session and see what the witness has to say about Masic. Let me just check. Yes, we are in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Judge Eser would like to put a question to you, Mr. Buric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Just to make clear. Now, since you talked about exaggeration and so on, now did you read this book which has on the title the name of Naser Oric, or did you read the other book either from Mr. Masic? Did you read them from the beginning to the end?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not see either book, either of the books. The first excerpt that I heard was here. But now I would like to say something about why I wouldn't allow Nijaz to write, if I may be allowed to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Again, let's go into private session now, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And thereupon immediately for a break for 30 minutes, starting from now.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I see. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Di Fazio.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Mr. Buric, I just have one more very minor topic about books. I'd like to show you another extract from the book that we were talking about Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. earlier, the Nijaz Masic book. It's a very brief matter. I've got copies for everyone, if Your Honours please. And it bears an ERN number 01099714. It's just an extract. And it's just a photograph, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Do Your Honours have it? It's just one page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Di Fazio, I heard you say "one page," but it's not one page that we have. Just for the record, let me say what we have. I have -- when I say "I," it means we because we have the same here. We have one page in the B/C/S version. It contains a photo.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And it has the ERN number 01099714.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And then the corresponding English translation. But then we were also given the following pages --

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: You don't need to concern yourselves about that, because I'm not intending to use that other material, and I'd ask that be withdrawn from you, because it's -- if I decide to use it, I'll produce it later. If Your Honours please, I'm only interested in that one page, the photograph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm collecting this.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I can understand how this happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's not a problem. We have enough papers. So if you spare us another four pages, you would be doing us a big favour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes. It's a very, very brief little issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Mr. Buric, this is just another page from the book of Mr. Nijaz Masic, and the only thing I want to ask you about is your photo that appears in there. You can set I think, can't you? The photo is pretty bad, and I can understand if you can't tell if it's you or not?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If the book is available, we can show him the book.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And then I'm sure the photo would be better.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Well, it may -- it would be better if it be signed. Perhaps I can -- I don't have it at hand now, and perhaps I can tend to it tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: In the meantime, I'll just go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Anyway, you can see underneath the caption, under photo, it says -- it's talking about you, Nesib Buric, son of Hasib, one of the activists in the resistance movement in Osmace, wounded in Srebrenica July 1995, and that -- and then there's the photograph. Do you know how your photograph came to be in the book?

utterances.speaker: Nesib Buric [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no idea. I did not give this photograph to Masic. I don't know where he got it from.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I'm not getting any translation, if Your Honours please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, I did. Mr. Jones --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. One moment, Mr. Buric.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I'm okay now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Are you receiving interpretation?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes, I think it might have been. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you need the witness to repeat or can you check it over on the transcript?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. That's answered the question. I'd tender it, if Your Honours please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I got the impression that the witness wanted to add something.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I didn't want to cut you off.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If you want to add something.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a photograph from the Srebrenica municipal office in Tuzla. I don't know. I mean, this is from Tuzla, the office where I worked, in the Srebrenica municipal office, which was located in Tuzla. But I really don't know how Masic got the photo.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Thank you very much. Can I get a number for this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. This will become Prosecution Exhibit P --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 568, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 568. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Buric. I think that's enough books for one afternoon. Let's move to another topic. You testified on Thursday and Friday regarding the impossibility of -- or not the impossibility, but the difficult of movement around the Srebrenica area in 1992 and early 1993. And I just want to remind you of one or two points in your evidence that you made. You were talking -- Mr. Jones was asking you questions about the ability -- communications and the ability to move around the area in May, June, and July of -- May -- April, May, and June of 1992. And you -- the upshot -- the essence of your evidence was that movement was almost impossible. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: Nesib Buric [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And were your comments confined to just the Osmace area or do you know that to be the case in other areas of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: Nesib Buric [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was primarily talking about Osmace, the Osmace region, which was intercepted with Serbian territories. And the same situation was in other places as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay. So would that be -- would that situation have applied further north, in areas, for example, around the Mocevici and Ratkovici, the difficulty of movement, I mean?

utterances.speaker: Nesib Buric [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Ratkovici is a Serb place, Mocevici was a Muslim place, but we had no communications with Mocevici. There was Mocevici, Brezani, Oparci, Crkvina. Until the end of July, they didn't or were not able to communicate with each other in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Would you say the same difficulties applied over towards Suceska, the general difficulty of movement for Muslim, Bosniak people?

utterances.speaker: Nesib Buric [Resumed]
utterances.text: Osmace did not have any communications with Suceska throughout the period, because all of those villages, Podjelova [phoen], Jasenova, and so on, all those villages. We did not have any information about Suceska.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: So I just want to be clear. Are you saying that you don't know what the situation was regarding the ability to move around for Bosniak or Muslim people in Suceska? Is that what you're saying, you just don't know?

utterances.speaker: Nesib Buric [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that Osmace did not have a physical connection with Suceska.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: All right. Okay. But do I take it from that fact that there wasn't a physical connection, that therefore you just don't know what situation applied -- what situation applied in Suceska as regards free movement?

utterances.speaker: Nesib Buric [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: You were answering questions on Friday about this topic, and you were talking about the decision to attack a place called Jezero. I'm not sure how you pronounce it.

utterances.speaker: Nesib Buric [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And you said - I'm looking at page 75, for Defence counsel: "I do apologise about before. What I said was: By the end of 1992 and the beginning of 1993, certain territories were linked up in that area, and that's why the decision was made on the 16th of January to attack this place called Jezero."

utterances.speaker: Nesib Buric [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Are you saying that that difficulty of movement applied equally throughout 1992 and early 1993 in the Jezero area?

utterances.speaker: Nesib Buric [Resumed]
utterances.text: With the fall of Brezani, things had changed. We had Podrid and Postolje on the other side, where Serbs from those villages were going, and people went looking for food there. And they realised that the village was empty. There was nobody there. So then there was some physical link which was established between Osmace and Kragljivoda.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let me -- I want to ask you, without actually going into the great detail, but tell me if you can answer this: Generally speaking, throughout 1992, from what you know and saw and heard and have learnt about what happened in that part of the country of Bosnia, would you say that it was very difficult for Muslims or Bosniaks to move about throughout all of 1992 and the early part of 1993? Would you say that?

utterances.speaker: Nesib Buric [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was very difficult to move about throughout that period, and those Serb villages from which the population withdrew, well, their patrols and units weren't there anyway and they set up ambushes. And so throughout that period up until 1993, any communication was extremely difficult.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: That's right. And in your evidence you said that one of the reasons, not the only reason, but one of the reasons to make movement difficult for the non-Serb population was the presence of Serb patrols. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: Nesib Buric [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: You also said that, however, in your evidence -- you also said in your evidence that, when you were talking about the movement of weapons, the movement of Serb weaponry, this, page 19. Mr. Jones asked you: "Did you receive any information as to where these trucks were coming from?" You were talking about trucks and the fellow called Milivoj, who used his trucking company. And you answered: "All the weapons came from the direction of Skelani." And you were asked: "And were trucks the only convoys that were used to bring in weapons into the area or were you aware of other means?" And then you said: "Yes. When they no longer felt that line, Skelani-Brezani, was safe, they started getting weapons from Fakovici en masse. And the transport took place by horseback and by roundabout mountain roads from Fakovici to Brezani, and also by JNA helicopters." And you went on to talk about helicopters.

utterances.speaker: Nesib Buric [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And then a little later, page --

utterances.speaker: Nesib Buric [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay. A little later, page -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Would Your Honours just give me a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Just one thing for the record. It was conveyances, not convoys. I noticed, rather than -- right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: That's right. I couldn't see the writing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you for the comment, Mr. Jones. You're correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And then, page 22, you were again answering questions about movement of weapons, and you said: "There were rumours in the surrounding Muslim villages that they saw that weapons were delivered to Ducici by helicopters from Fakovici, and as to Brezani, we knew that they were getting weapons and that those weapons were being transported on horseback from Fakovici, weapons and ammunition, that is, and they went through the forests and creeks, et cetera, in a roundabout way, anyway." And you later in the day again made reference to this secretive Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. mode of the Serbs moving arms. Why did the Serbs have to adopt that method of transport if they controlled all movement in the area? Why did they have to bring in weapons in roundabout ways?

utterances.speaker: Nesib Buric [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nobody said that they were using those roads, as you say, in that way. Since those were villages which were mixed, Muslim and Serb, and in those places where there were Muslim villages in between, I mean, they didn't do it out in the open in order for the Muslims to be able to see it. They went in a roundabout way and to get arms and weapons they used trucks and horses and vans and helicopters. Not from Fakovici, as you said, directly to Ducici by helicopters, but from Serbia, I said that they were crossing over from Serbia, from Skelani. I mean, the helicopters did. And then from Fakovici to Ratkovici and Ducici, it was all transported on horseback. So the reason for them to take a roundabout route was that there were Muslim villages in between. They had to -- otherwise they would have had to travel through Muslim villages, and they didn't want the Muslims to see what they were up to, and that's why they went the long way round.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes, but in April, May, June, the Serbs couldn't have cared less about concealing the movement of weapons from Bosniaks or Muslims. War had already broken out. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: Nesib Buric [Resumed]
utterances.text: They didn't dare travel through Muslim villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: That's what I'm interested in. And is it the case that they didn't dare travel through Muslim villages because Bosniaks -- hang on.

utterances.speaker: Nesib Buric [Resumed]
utterances.text: They did not --

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay. I'll put my question again. Is it the case that they didn't dare travel past Muslim villages because there was emerging in those months a -- an organised Muslim resistance and they were getting better, Muslims and Bosniaks were getting better and more effective at fighting back? Is that the reason they had to take their horses and transport their weapons in roundabout ways?

utterances.speaker: Nesib Buric [Resumed]
utterances.text: We have to get one thing straight. March and April were the time when Serbs made use of the Muslim territories. There was still a certain amount of freedom everywhere, and they could travel freely with those lorries. Nobody would have checked their trucks, et cetera. But after the murders of Meha and Bahrudin, that, of course, triggered off panic and therefore the Serbs didn't dare travel through Muslim villages again because presumably they must have been afraid as well, and so that's why they took this roundabout route. And the most convenient way to travel was on horseback

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'm just reading the transcript of the 8th, and the references to dates there are all April 1992. Just to be absolutely clear, it was in April 1992, that this was going on, the arming of Ducici, and then the questions followed about helicopters, et cetera. And above that as well, he was speaking about General Zivanovic and he's saying April 1992. So those answers were given in relation to April 1992, and I think it's mischaracterising it to say he was talking about April, May, June, 1992. The matter could perhaps be resolved by simply asking the witness what period this -- they were taking roundabout routes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think you're right, because I vividly remember that your question and his answer at the time was limited to that particular period of time, which is just pre-war, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If I remember well. The term "pre-war" or before the war, was used. Correct me if I'm wrong, but I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'll have to check, but I think so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Di Fazio. I think it's easy. This can be dealt with in a pretty easy manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes, I think so, Your Honour. I understand what --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The concern showed by Mr. Jones is perfectly legitimate.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: So is it the case that after April there wasn't any need for the Serbs to take roundabout routes to transport their weapons, roundabout routes through the forest and so on?

utterances.speaker: Nesib Buric [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've stated it quite clearly. Up until the 13th of April, the murders of Meho and Bahrudin, the Serbs used to make use of the asphalt roads, used the same trucks and lorries that they used to drive when they did work in agriculture. But after the murders of Bahrudin and Meho they started to hide a little bit what they were up to and they started using those secondary roads. It was later, after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: When? When did they start to use those secondary roads?

utterances.speaker: Nesib Buric [Resumed]
utterances.text: We managed, by the end of April, or in May -- well, we discovered, as I said, that there was a convoy on horseback from Fakovici taking arms to the sector of Brezani.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay. Well, by the end of April, certainly by the end -- by the beginning of May, hostilities had broken out, hadn't they, in the Srebrenica area?

utterances.speaker: Nesib Buric [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is to say, after the murders of Meho and Bahrudin. They committed those murders and we saw that incident as the beginning of hostilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay. But could you explain why the Serbs felt it necessary to use secondary roads towards the end of April and/or May? I mean, bearing in mind all of your evidence of their massive superiority that you've given in terms of weapons and the assistance they were receiving from Serbia and so on, why would it have been necessary for the Serbs to conceal in the slightest movement of arms?

utterances.speaker: Nesib Buric [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. They should be asked perhaps why they felt they had to hide.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Land-mines were another reason you say that Bosniaks and Muslims encountered difficulties in moving around freely. Do you recall that evidence?

utterances.speaker: Nesib Buric [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And you said that -- I think this is a fair summary, that the Serbs mined their own villages and the areas close to their villages, and sometimes when their villages were too far apart, they would mine the area in between their villages. Do you recall that evidence?

utterances.speaker: Nesib Buric [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Why -- do you know why the Serbs mined their own villages?

utterances.speaker: Nesib Buric [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Sorry. We did not hear what the witness just said.

utterances.speaker: Nesib Buric [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that they were shelling their own village. I never mentioned mining. They placed land-mines around the Serb villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Sorry. Perhaps we're misunderstanding each other. I think we do understand each other. They placed mines around their villages, didn't they, around their own villages?

utterances.speaker: Nesib Buric [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, around their own villages. That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay. And that's a defensive tactic, isn't it, to have a mine -- to have a minefield around your own village? It's for protection, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: Nesib Buric [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not really for protection, in fact. Professional military units, all branches were involved, and they were involved in placing the land-mines, providing arms, bringing in the artillery and the air force. So they were involved in every way, and also some special units. And they used special tactics, that is, starving people and making them exhausted, et cetera. So a special type of warfare was used. And all those different types of warfare was used in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He hasn't actually answered your question, Mr. Di Fazio. Mr. Buric, look at me, please, and give me a straight answer. Why were the Serbs mining the perimeter of the villages? Why would they place land-mines around their villages? What was the purpose of that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was not enough population in the Serb villages, because 80 per cent of the population in the municipality of Srebrenica was Muslim. So in whatever area they felt they did not have sufficient cover from a military point of view, they used the land-mines and the artillery. They felt that if you had five -- four or five houses standing together, it would be a village. So there was 80 per cent of the Muslim population and 20 per cent of the Serb population, and out of that 20 per cent, 10 per cent had houses in Serbia. And so they made up for the fact that they didn't have a lot of population by laying the land-mines.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Does that satisfy you, Mr. Di Fazio, or do you want to pursue it any further? I am not going to pursue it any further.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay. So is it the case that you think that the fact that the Serbs were -- speaking demographically, in a minority in the area, made them scared, so they mined their own villages? Is that a fair summary or not?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Again, you're going to confuse him. When you say "they mined their own villages --"

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Mined the areas around their villages.

utterances.speaker: Nesib Buric [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, no. A land-mine is a type of weapon, in much the same way that they used the artillery weapons and rifles, they used mines as well. It is an offensive weapon. They used it for the purposes of destruction, not just around the villages. Jezero is not a village. They had three rows of mines there. So they did not come to Fakovici and so on, they would get to the Muslim village of Zanjevo and they placed land-mines there as well. Wherever they felt that Muslim civilians were likely to walk by to look for food, they would place land-mines.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: So you're talking about the deliberate laying of mines in areas where they expected Serb --

utterances.speaker: Nesib Buric [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: -- to walk in their search for food -- sorry, Muslims to walk in their search for food, so that they would be either killed or maimed; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Nesib Buric [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Voljevica is a purely Muslim village, and the fact that the civilians went to their fields in order to collect food led them to place land-mines in the cornfields, in the barns. It was their intention to kill and maim Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay. But that's the laying of mines in their fields and around their villages; is that correct? And the killings and maimings, which undoubtedly occurred, result --

utterances.speaker: Nesib Buric [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. What I have just said --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honours, sorry. It's just the "their" is ambiguous as well. If might be confusing the witness. If we could say in the Muslim fields and around Muslim villages. He says, "explain Voljevica being a Muslim village," otherwise it is ambiguous.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I would agree with you there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: All right. Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did say Muslim villages. Let me Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. clarify this once again. Voljevica is a purely Muslim village and those were Muslim fields. And another proof of that: When we talked about the dead bodies in Fakovici, they laid land-mines there. I mean, they were in no danger whatsoever, but did it intentionally to kill as many Muslims as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's cut this short, because I think basically we are just digressing. Would you agree with me, Mr. Buric, that the placing of land-mines around villages -- around Serbian villages, in particular, was meant for both defensive and offensive purposes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I just point this out once again. It was not just the Serb villages we are talking about. They laid mines in the Muslim villages as well. Wherever they felt that the population might be going at the crossings, at the access part through their barns, et cetera, it was simply to kill people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm not going to pursue it any further. I was clear in my question that I was referring to Serb villages. So if you want to pursue the matter any further, please do so, by all means, Mr. Di Fazio. Otherwise we'll move to something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: We will. I just want to put a proposition.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I suggest to you that the Serbs who lived in their villages in the Srebrenica area mined the approaches to their own villages, primarily as a defensive manoeuvre, and did so because they realised that there was a growing and organised military resistance on the part of Bosniaks and Muslims.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Divide the question into two parts, please. I mean, first ask him the first part of the question. And if he answers you in the affirmative, then ask him why would they use that tactic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I suggest to you that the Serbs mined the approaches to their villages as a defensive ploy, a defensive move.

utterances.speaker: Nesib Buric [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already mentioned this. 80 per cent of the population is Muslim. So now, if you look at the map of Srebrenica, 80 per cent of Muslim villages are actually in the middle of land-mines. Let me just make this clear. 80 per cent of Muslim villages are in the middle of minefields created by Serbs. Perhaps humanitarian organisations have these maps indicating where the land-mines are. 80 per cent of Muslim villages are actually surrounded by Serb land-mines.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Let's move to another topic. You mentioned that you were a member of an organisation related -- that did work on behalf of war veterans. Did you ever -- what's the name of that organisation?

utterances.speaker: Nesib Buric [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am a member of the association of war invalids and veterans of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And when did you become a member of that organisation, that association?

utterances.speaker: Nesib Buric [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is a voluntary organisation. I mean, anyone can set up an association of this sort, but I think it must be 1997 or 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And are you still a member?

utterances.speaker: Nesib Buric [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Is Mr. Oric a member of that organisation, that association?

utterances.speaker: Nesib Buric [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay. Do you know Mr. Oric? Obviously you've said that -- I gather from the way you've been talking that you know of him. What I really would like --

utterances.speaker: Nesib Buric [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: When did you first meet him?

utterances.speaker: Nesib Buric [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first time that I met him was some point at the beginning of April, the end of March/beginning of April 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And where was that? Can you recall?

utterances.speaker: Nesib Buric [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And how did you come to meet him on that occasion? Can you remember?

utterances.speaker: Nesib Buric [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were gathering in the square in town. This was before demilitarisation, and there were daily attacks by the Serbs. And I saw him somewhere there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And when you met him on that occasion, did you find out what he did in the Srebrenica area?

utterances.speaker: Nesib Buric [Resumed]
utterances.text: As to what we knew about Naser at Osmace and what we appreciated about him was the ambush for the Arkan men at Potocari, because they used to pillage and loot and kill. And in his village, they stopped them and they could no longer get through. I mean, the Arkan's men. And that's how I knew of him. And I remember that. So that was my first impression of him.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And that must have given you the impression of a fairly courageous and resourceful man who was able to resist someone as -- like Arkan.

utterances.speaker: Nesib Buric [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I of course appreciated his courage, and we all welcomed and appreciated his courage.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Had you known about him prior to meeting him in April of 1993, for example, in 1992?

utterances.speaker: Nesib Buric [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we had heard -- I don't know the exact date when, but we heard that Naser staged an ambush against these Arkan's men. But I think it was in July 1992 that we heard about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Sorry, would Your Honours just bear with me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: When did you hear about this ambush with -- sorry. It was July 1992 that you heard about the ambush that --

utterances.speaker: Nesib Buric [Resumed]
utterances.text: June or July. I can't really tell you exactly. I think it was in June or July 1992 that we heard about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: All right. And did that, as far as you're aware, anyway, as far as you're aware in the area of Osmace, mean that Mr. Oric acquired some fame in Srebrenica, in the Osmace area?

utterances.speaker: Nesib Buric [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Following -- once you heard about his role in this Arkan business in June or July of 1992, did he become more famous in your area?

utterances.speaker: Nesib Buric [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, nothing special. We just heard that he had staged an ambush. This was about 20 kilometres away from us, and it was a very long way away, as far as we were concerned. It didn't really mean anything to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And that's the only time you heard about him in 1992?

utterances.speaker: Nesib Buric [Resumed]
utterances.text: That I heard of him for the first time?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes. That's the only time you heard mention of him, was in 19 -- June or July of 1992, when you heard about his role in the Arkan business?

utterances.speaker: Nesib Buric [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we also heard in early 1993 is that he was holding the lines at Potocari, that Serbs were trying daily and attacking Srebrenica from Zuti Most, and that Naser was in Potocari and did not allow the line to be moved, and that he was very brave in holding that line. We heard that that part that he was holding, Potocari, was very stable, and we heard that he was brave.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: All right. Do you know a fellow named Nedzib, Nedzib Habibovic, Nedzib Habibovic?

utterances.speaker: Nesib Buric [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I know Nedzib Delic, but not Habibovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Can the witness be shown P21, thanks. It's on Sanction.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I just want to very quickly take you through this document. It won't take long, Mr. Buric. From what you know of Mr. Oric, are some of those details correct, his father's name is Dzemal, his mother's name is Hata?

utterances.speaker: Nesib Buric [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went to his late father's funeral, but I really don't know what his name was. I know that he was a Muslim from Potocari. I don't know when he was born. I know that he was a policeman in Belgrade, a soldier. I mean, I found that out later.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: When did you go to his late father's funeral? When was that?

utterances.speaker: Nesib Buric [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. Maybe it was in 2003 or 2004. I really don't know. Maybe it was in 2001, 2002. I really don't know exactly what year it was, but I know that I was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. And were you invited or did you just go along to pay your respects?

utterances.speaker: Nesib Buric [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It's not our custom to invite people to the funeral. But all of us exiled people from Srebrenica have this custom of going to the funeral of one of our people.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay. Now, look at the other detail under number 7. It says "Srebrenica, OS commander." Have you got any idea what that might be referring to in this document?

utterances.speaker: Nesib Buric [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know that he was a commander of the armed forces. I assumed that he had a group of his own and that he was in charge in Potocari. In 1993, I didn't know that he was a commander of the armed forces. I can state with a lot of certainty that I didn't even know that there were any armed forces in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Can the witness be shown P22.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: This document is apparently dated March of 1994, and it's to the command of the 8th Operations Group Srebrenica, and it refers to a number of decorations. And it says that Mr. Oric is the recipient of the Golden Lily wartime decoration. Do you know anything about that? Firstly, did you know that he received any such decoration? And secondly, if you do know, do you know what he received it for?

utterances.speaker: Nesib Buric [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that he received that. I would just like to say one thing, though, Your Honours. In our B and H army, where units were functioning, in Tuzla, Sarajevo, then for some exceptional achievement, you would be decorated for downing an aeroplane or destroying some artillery weapons or capturing a tank or something. So for that you would get the Golden Lily. So I mean, I could just say that this is not the way it was. We're talking about up until the year 2000. When I was working for the Srebrenica municipality, you don't receive a decoration like this. I had asked for some information to be provided about Naser Oric, and there is no information, appropriate information for Naser Oric, because then it would be accompanied by the proper paperwork. And this decoration, as far as him being awarded it, was never accompanied by the appropriate paperwork.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Do you know how many other people in the Srebrenica area received the Golden Lily award?

utterances.speaker: Nesib Buric [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about the region of Srebrenica, but I know that people from Srebrenica, about 20 people from Srebrenica, throughout the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina, received the Golden Lily. So these were people who had lived in the area of Srebrenica before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. I've finished with that exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Can the witness be shown P32.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I don't want to spend long on this. Just -- I'll tell you what it's about. It's a Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina Supreme Command Staff of the armed forces, dated 15th of April, 1993, and it's an order apparently by the -- by Sefer Halilovic, Chief of the Supreme Staff of the armed forces. And there's a special tribute being paid to various defenders, various -- commendation to some units, commendation to some institutions. And then, lastly, commendations to some individuals, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. including Naser Oric. Do you know what that commendation was about? If you don't, that's fine.

utterances.speaker: Nesib Buric [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that period, and as I see in the heading, the 15th of March, 1993, there was a general offensive against Srebrenica. When about 90 per cent of the territory had fallen, there was fierce fighting at the approaches to the town of Srebrenica in that period, very close to the centre. And we had managed to keep the Serb forces from entering, from doing what they did in 1995. There was a lot of people in the town at the time, and we did not allow them to enter. So I assume that this is why Naser was commended in this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: But you don't actually know?

utterances.speaker: Nesib Buric [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was chaos in that period, from the 23rd of March, from Kragljivoda, Osmace, there was fierce fighting going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I understand all that. I've heard what you've said. All -- it's a very simple question: Do you actually know the reason that he got that commendation, the actual reason? If you don't know it, I'm --

utterances.speaker: Nesib Buric [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Before we leave this document, because the document, at the top left-hand corner says 15th April. Your question, of course, referred to the same date, 15th April. But in his answer, the witness mentioned 15th of March, 1993. Could someone check with the B/C/S version whether we have 15th March or 15th April 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I did not mention the 15th of May. This was a continuation of the Serb offensive from the 23rd of March.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It makes it even more confused. Because the confusion that seemed apparent at least is whether it was -- whether the witness actually said 15th March 1993, and what shows up in the B/C/S version of this document, and now we have, at least in the interpretation, 15th May of 1993. So can someone -- if it is on Sanction, could we have the first page. One moment, Mr. Buric. Could we just have the first page of the document in the B/C/S version. So it's 15th of April. Okay. All right. 15th of April. Let's move. Stop. Finished. Next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Mr. Buric, am I correct that this is your position regarding

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIC
utterances.text: You never heard of him being -- holding any position as overall wartime commander of soldiers or fighters in the Srebrenica area?

utterances.speaker: Nesib Buric [Resumed]
utterances.text: I state with a great degree of certainty that he could not have been a commander, and he was not a commander over the whole territory of the Srebrenica region. He could have been a commander of the Potocari group, however.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And is it your position that there was - I'm not speaking about Mr. Oric now - but there was just no one in overall command of any fighters or soldiers in the Srebrenica area; there were just isolated, individual groups of fighters who may or may not have had a commander, but no command structure of any description at all, and most of all, no single, overall commander?

utterances.speaker: Nesib Buric [Resumed]
utterances.text: He could not have been a commander, and he was not a commander of all the units or groups, as you say, in the Srebrenica municipality. There was no one who would be an overall commander, as you put it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Do you know of a publication called Dani, in Srebrenica -- in Bosnia, sorry.

utterances.speaker: Nesib Buric [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nasi Dani doesn't exist in Srebrenica, but there is a weekly magazine called Masi [phoen] Dani and Slobodna Bosna. There is a weekly Nasi [phoen] Dani published in the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And do you know that one of the founders and first editors of this magazine was a chap named Senad Pecanin? Have you ever heard of him?

utterances.speaker: Nesib Buric [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Were you ever interviewed by any journalists or reporters or writers from that newspaper or magazine or weekly, whatever is the right description?

utterances.speaker: Nesib Buric [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. Perhaps it was maybe Hasan Hadzic. Several people came when I was working in the Srebrenica municipal office, but I really can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I think you might be right. I'll show you a document that I want to -- I've got copies here. This has got no ERN numbers, if Your Honours please. For the purposes of the Trial Chamber, this material was obtained from the Internet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: How far does the first publication of this weekly go, Mr. Di Fazio?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I'm not sure I understand Your Honour's question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: When was it first published?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: The actual weekly?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, this Dani.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: This particular one or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. This magazine or weekly or whatever it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: How far does it go back?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I don't know personally. But I understand, and I'm only reporting what is my understanding --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The witness just mentioned that he was sort of -- several people used to visit him when he was in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I see, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What I'm trying to find out is what period of time is he referring to and whether this weekly was in existence then already. So this is what I basically want to know. Yes, Ms. Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the witness said "people came to see me while I was working," but he never said that these visits took place when he was in Srebrenica. Witness, did I understand you properly that you did not say that you were visited in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I said that these visits were at the Srebrenica municipal office in Tuzla, and it was after 1996.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That means that line 12 of the previous page stands to be corrected, because there is a specific mention of Srebrenica. I don't know. I mean, I take your word for it, Madam Vidovic, but -- yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: All right. Now, you've got the B/C/S? Good. It's entitled --

utterances.speaker: Nesib Buric [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: It's entitled "Humane transfer of population Dani, Sarajevo, Bosnia, on January 18 -- 19 -- 1999, by Hasan Hadzic." Now, what I want you to do is just turn the pages over until you get to what is obviously the -- purports to be an interview with you. Can you find that? I think you'll find yours -- it's got grey on it, grey over the writing.

utterances.speaker: Nesib Buric [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And you're being apparently interviewed by this fellow. First question is: Were you indeed interviewed by Mr. Hasan Hadzic, from Dani, around that time, January of 1999?

utterances.speaker: Nesib Buric [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And it's pretty easy to make your way through the document, or the interview. And it -- yes. It says that you're the deputy mayor for social security of war veterans and disabled persons in Srebrenica. Do you see that? Can you tell me yes or no? Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: Nesib Buric [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Deputy mayor for social security at the Tuzla office. So with the fall in 1995 and the arrival at the free territory municipal office of the Srebrenica region -- was formed in Tuzla where it worked to provide social security for war veterans and disabled persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. Last question -- sorry. The second-to-last question that apparently you were asked is a question that says: "What hurts the most?" And you then go on to give an answer about events concerning veterans. And then you say, at least what I have here in English: "All of them, starting with Naser Oric, who honourably led us and whom we will always trust, mostly still have the same rank they had in Srebrenica." That's the only part that I'm asking you about now. My first question is this: Did you say that to Mr. Hadzic, or words to that effect, that Naser Oric honourably led you and whom you will always trust?

utterances.speaker: Nesib Buric [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just one moment so that we can clarify certain things. With the demilitarisation of Srebrenica on the 18th of April, they received - I don't know - as far as I can recall, they received some kind of letter from Tuzla to form an operations group, a division - I don't know exactly, because I was in the civilian structures - to form it and then - we're now talking about after the demilitarisation - they, and I'm not really going to deal with that, they made some kind of structure, schedule, units, commanders. But this fragment, excerpt, is something -- these are my private thoughts, because it talks about the expulsion of disabled people from Srebrenica, from their apartments. And we, these invalids, disabled persons, addressed President Alija Izetbegovic in a letter, and our -- through our representative, Aldo Smajlovic, that if he couldn't at least provide the basic accommodation for the expellees from Srebrenica, then he should make it possible for us to get out. I'm thinking of treatment, because I spent a lot of time in the hospital. So this is all referring to the period after the demilitarisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please, repeat the question. And Mr. Buric, please try to answer the question and just the question, without giving other information, for the time being. And then we'll move to the rest of the information, if you are asked about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: You see, my question, Mr. Buric, is -- it's very simple, okay. On the face of it, Mr. Hadzic asked you: "What hurts the most?" And you gave an answer. Now, I'm not being callous, but I'm not interested in the actual subject. What I'm interested in is part of your answer. And it says: "All of them, starting with Naser Oric, who honourably led us and whom we will always trust, mostly still have the same rank they had in Srebrenica," and then you go on to talk about other matters. Now, all I want to know is this. It's very simple. Did you say to Mr. Hadzic those words or words to those effect, namely, that Naser Oric honourably led you and that he's a man whom "we will always trust"?

utterances.speaker: Nesib Buric [Resumed]
utterances.text: I probably did say it. But I'm thinking of the period after the demilitarisation. So this is the -- making units or putting units together in the area of Srebrenica after the demilitarisation, and it was after the 18th of April, 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Your microphone, Mr. Di Fazio.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: What did he do in the period of post-demilitarisation to honourably lead you? Do you know what you might have been referring to? Not just the creation of army units, surely.

utterances.speaker: Nesib Buric [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went to the civilian structures of the Srebrenica municipality and they -- I don't know what they were doing then there in the military structures. I, on the 1st of May, 1993, started to work in the civilian structures, and Srebrenica was a demilitarised zone. Disarming occurred. They ordered the creation of the 2nd Corps, of an operations group. They Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. placed Naser as the commander of -- there was a division. So I'm talking about the demilitarised zone, about the disarming of the units, the handing over of the weapons. So all of his command duties are within the demilitarised zone area.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: So we're not to read that as Naser Oric honourably leading you in the period of 1992 up to April 1992, to demilitarisation. That's not what you're talking about when you say that he honourably led you. You're talking about other matters that happened after there was a peace of some sort following demilitarisation?

utterances.speaker: Nesib Buric [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It all refers to demilitarisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I see. Thank you for that explanation. You were asked a question, if you go back in the interview now, just go backwards, by apparently the same journalist, and the question was: "What about war veteran organisations? Have you contacted them?" And then on -- you apparently gave the answer that follows, and it seems that you said that: "On May 8, 1992, with 20 guys, I was the first Bosniak to break through to the Drina River. And in my battalion, out of 320 fighters, 280 died during the war." First question is this: Did you say that or words to that effect in --

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Not for the time being. Let him answer the question, please. The question refers as to whether he has made this statement to the writer. Let him finish first. Let him finish first, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the interpretation for the witness is incorrect. The witness is receiving incorrect translation. Could perhaps the witness read the text? I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I'm happy to do that, if Your Honours would --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Di Fazio, please refer the witness to the particular sentence in the paragraph and repeat your question. I mean, he can read it himself. It's not a question of interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: It's only a little bit that I'm interested in. It's only a small -- well, perhaps the first -- in English, Mr. Buric, I'm -- let's do it this way. Find the question that starts, that says: "What about war veteran organisations? Have you contacted them?" And then carefully read your entire answer that follows and let us know when you've completed it.

utterances.speaker: Nesib Buric [Resumed]
utterances.text: The question is clear, and I'm going to give you an answer. My area, Kragljivoda --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. You haven't heard the question as yet, Mr. Buric. And the question, very simply put, if I understood you well, is whether the words that you have read here, whether you actually said those words to Mr. Hadzic or not. For the time being that's the --

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Or words to that effect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Or words to that effect. If you remember having said those words, say so. If you don't remember having said those words, say so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The complaint was that Mr. Di Fazio's reading of the English text was being wrongly interpreted in B/C/S. This is the complaint of Ms. Vidovic, if I understand well.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Your Honour, it would be better for the witness to read the actual text in this sentence which says: Well, I did not ... And so on. Because the interpretation that he received was totally incorrect. Do believe me. We can check it out later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I do believe you, Ms. Vidovic. But I take it -- have you read this paragraph now, Mr. Buric, or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. And do you remember -- do you recall having said those words to Mr. Hadzic or words to that effect?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I explain what the reference is?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: First, please answer the question whether you recall having spoken those words to Mr. Hadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Then your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. So you never said anything like that. Okay. Well, I just want to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He said he doesn't recall. He is not saying that he never did. He's saying that he doesn't recall. I was careful in what I asked.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I just explain one point?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have the exact data as to the number killed from the village of Osmace, so you can see quite clearly that the figure here, 280, is incorrect, because in the course of combat activities, about 40 people were killed at Osmace. And we've got a list with names and surnames. About 40 people from killed from Osmace, and not 280. And what about this 320? Yes, there were about 20 lads armed with rifles. But -- and about 50 people from the group that operated in that area throughout the war. It wasn't 320. And as to these numbers, 320 and 260 or whatever, even according to the structure after demilitarisation, there were not 300 able-bodied men who could have been members of the military service. So it is incorrect, because we've got the exact data as to how many people were killed from Osmace.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay. So you don't recall ever saying that, and furthermore, you say it doesn't make sense because of those numbers you've just told us; is that right?

utterances.speaker: Nesib Buric [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm giving you the correct figures. Up until demilitarisation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Buric, just answer the question. It's a simple question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, this information is incorrect.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay. Further down, about halfway through your answer, I've got a phrase there that you apparently said: "No one can deny that we set up a large, free territory." It's about halfway through the answer. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: Nesib Buric [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Did you say that or words to that effect to the journalist?

utterances.speaker: Nesib Buric [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And if I may take you to that earlier portion of your answer there, I was asking you about: "Did you ever use the word "battalion" at any time with this journalist, Hasan Hadzic, when giving the interview, referring to people from your area, word "battalion"?

utterances.speaker: Nesib Buric [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall mentioning the term "battalion."

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you very much for answering those questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: If Your Honours please, I tender the exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This will be Prosecution Exhibit P569. Madam. Vidovic, I'm sorry I dealt with you the way I did, but when I tell you "stop," obviously you're required to stop. If it's a question of interpretation, just say it's a question of interpretation, and then I will review my decision, obviously. But the way there was a clear misunderstanding, all right? Thank you. Yes, Mr. Di Fazio.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: You said in evidence on Thursday and Friday, you were talking about your group in Osmace, and I can't remember the precise numbers, but I think you said about 50 or so men armed with about 20 or 21 hunting rifles. That's correct, isn't it? Did that situation change at all? Did more men come and join this group that you've talked about in Osmace throughout 1992?

utterances.speaker: Nesib Buric [Resumed]
utterances.text: Up until 1993 and the withdrawal of the refugee population, that group earned about 50 rifles, up to 90 people, maximum, were engaged in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: So it increased by only a small number, about another 40 or so men, later in 1992?

utterances.speaker: Nesib Buric [Resumed]
utterances.text: It increased maybe 100 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: You also said that it bore absolutely no semblance whatsoever to a military unit of any description, and you recall Mr. Jones took you through your questions and -- some questions establishing that you didn't have barracks, you didn't have a commander, everyone joined voluntarily, whether they wanted to stay or not was a matter for them. Do you recall that evidence?

utterances.speaker: Nesib Buric [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not clear to me what you meant, who was supposed to stay where.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: All I'm saying is -- sorry. When you were answering questions about this group in Osmace, Mr. Jones asked you questions about whether there was any structure to this group and you -- and anything that might make it resemble a military unit. And you pointed out that they had no barracks, you received no weapons, there was no commander, and that people were there voluntarily, they could come and go as they wished. Is that -- do you recall that evidence?

utterances.speaker: Nesib Buric [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Well, there were no military units. Everything was on a voluntary basis, without any arms and without any coercion. So whoever wanted to could act to save their lives. So it was only volunteers and there was no military structure whatsoever. There were no platoons, companies, battalions, whatever.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And did a leader of this group ever emerge, even in a natural way, someone who simply seemed to take over, so to speak, and start to lead the group?

utterances.speaker: Nesib Buric [Resumed]
utterances.text: What we did, the locals, we would choose the most stable person, for example, somebody who had worked in the police force for a long time, and we decided that perhaps he should be our leader. And he was Atif Krdzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And how did that come about? Was it a village meeting or was it put to a vote? How did he emerge?

utterances.speaker: Nesib Buric [Resumed]
utterances.text: There wasn't a meeting or anything. I did say earlier on that Osmace is made up of six hamlets and my hamlet, Mahala, was the biggest. We had the majority, therefore, and therefore we suggested Atif Krdzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I just want to briefly show you a document, P80. Defence counsel showed you this document last week and he focussed your attention on paragraph 3, or heading number 3. You can see, it's under the topic of first formation structure. Number 1 is TO Potocari; number 2 is TO Suceska; and number 3 is TO Osmace. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: Nesib Buric [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I think, after having been shown the document, your position is that this is not a document that really bears any resemblance to reality. Is that fair enough?

utterances.speaker: Nesib Buric [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It bears no resemblance to reality.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And under number 3, you'd agree, would you, that there was never a unit called A3, with 121 conscripts? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: Nesib Buric [Resumed]
utterances.text: The last time I had said that in March 1993, when those combat activities were over, that even then there were not as many as 120 people at Osmace. So throughout my testimony I referred to a group of about 50 men, up until the period of time toward the end of 1992, when the number was increased.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: To what sort of numbers was it increased at the end of 1992?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think he's answered that question. He said doubled, roughly.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Nesib Buric [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were perhaps 90 men in the group then.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. Usher, I've finished with P80.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Is Krdzic a fairly common name in the Osmace area, a fairly common surname?

utterances.speaker: Nesib Buric [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is. That's the only area that you come across that name.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And what about your surname, Buric? Is that a fairly common name in Osmace?

utterances.speaker: Nesib Buric [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is, only in Osmace.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: What about Hukic?

utterances.speaker: Nesib Buric [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are Hukics in a couple of villages, and in Osmace too.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: What about Hasanovic?

utterances.speaker: Nesib Buric [Resumed]
utterances.text: In almost every village. There are quite a few Hasanovics.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Handzic?

utterances.speaker: Nesib Buric [Resumed]
utterances.text: In a couple of villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Jahic.

utterances.speaker: Nesib Buric [Resumed]
utterances.text: The same, a couple of villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Delic?

utterances.speaker: Nesib Buric [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very many.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Would Your Honours just bear with me? Thank you. I'd like to produce a document to the witness, if Your Honours please. I've got English copies, and I can put the B/C/S on the screen. We've got B/C/S copies coming down and they should be available many in a matter of minutes. Is that okay with Your Honours? The witness will be able to see it on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's okay with us, I suppose, if it's okay with the Defence too.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: We don't have an ERN. So if we could know the ERN and the date as well, if possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Is there a date, just to check we've got the right --

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: That's fine with us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So, Usher, please, I want to make sure that the witness has got on his monitor the B/C/S version. And please verify that and confirm it to us. And the English version can be put on the ELMO, and we can try and follow from there. And if there are any discrepancies, then obviously please let us know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Firstly, if Your Honours please, just a question of translation. I'd like you to look, if Your Honours please, to the top of the document, as it progresses through, and look at that where it says "Osmace," you see a thick black writing. Okay? Can we see the next page, please. Start at the beginning and scroll through. I wonder if Your Honours would look at that. It's only a minor point. I just want to clarify it before I ask the witness any questions about this. All right? So there's the first page. Now if we could see the second page. Sorry, that is the second page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What we are looking at on this page now is what the first --

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: The second one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Number 17.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: 75, okay. Let's look at 76, the one ending 76. Let's look at the one ending 77. And let's look at the one ending 78. And finally, the one ending 79. If Your Honours please, that's -- to me is an "A" and a 3, A3. The translation says "Unit 43." I think that's wrong and I'd like to point that out to you. That's all I wanted to point out and raise with you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay? Okay. Of course, we are not telling you that it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: No, but I raise that and that's the Prosecution's position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Look at the names on that first page with -- bearing ERN number that ends 5774. Do you recognise those people?

utterances.speaker: Nesib Buric [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And turn over to -- or rather, electronically I'll turn the page so we have 7 -- 5775. Do you see that? And there are some names there. Under number 25 is, I think, maybe your name, Nesib Buric. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: Nesib Buric [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Your father's name was Hasib?

utterances.speaker: Nesib Buric [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: 18th October 1963. That's your date of birth?

utterances.speaker: Nesib Buric [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: All right. And do you recognise the names of the other characters set out there?

utterances.speaker: Nesib Buric [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. Next page, please. Do you recognise those people, the names there?

utterances.speaker: Nesib Buric [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And next page, please.

utterances.speaker: Nesib Buric [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And the next few pages, if you'd just tell us, once you recognise --

utterances.speaker: Nesib Buric [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Next one.

utterances.speaker: Nesib Buric [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Until we get to the end. Next one?

utterances.speaker: Nesib Buric [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And the names at 121, Jahic Mehmeda, Mehmed, do you see that?

utterances.speaker: Nesib Buric [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: On the face of this document, it appears to refer to the existence of some sort of military unit called Osmace Territorial Defence TO unit, I say, A, "A" for "apple," 3. Was there ever such a unit in existence?

utterances.speaker: Nesib Buric [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, definitely not, never. This is simply a census of the inhabitants of Osmace, and, most definitely -- I mean, this is the census, and, most definitely, only about 50 guys -- I think we should look at the date, because this must have been drawn up during demilitarisation. But if you look at the period of time between April and May, there were about 50 lads there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think I have about five minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Six or seven minutes. It's up to you. But we need to stop at 6.30, because I promised everyone that we would.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it seems to me that I heard the witness say: "We have to look at the date," and I fail to see this in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, and I also said that this was a census of the population of Osmace, and not a reference to any group of people being active or operational in the field.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Madam Vidovic. And thank you, Mr. Buric.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: You were shown --

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Can the witness be shown P80.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Are we going to give this a number?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: In a moment. I can do it straight away, if we finish. Sorry, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This document that we see on the monitor will become Prosecution Exhibit P570 [Realtime transcript read in error "578"]. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: It's only a minor point, Mr. Buric, but P80, which I showed you earlier on, has a part under heading number 3, TO Osmace, a reference to something called Osmace Company A3, with 121 conscripts, as P578 seems to have. Does that alter your view of P80 as being a document unfounded in reality, or not?

utterances.speaker: Nesib Buric [Resumed]
utterances.text: We can see that the date is the 19th of September, 1993. So I don't know where this was drawn up within demilitarisation period. But I can definitely state that up until demilitarisation, this is not something that had existed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I think that would be an appropriate time, if Your Honours please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I noticed that -- thank you, and I noticed that the document that you were expecting --

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: It's just arrived.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's just arrived. You'll tender it tomorrow? All right. Are you happy with that, Ms. -- Madam Vidovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I'm being told that when I said five exhibits, this will become P570. Apparently it shows 578 in the transcript. That's line 7 of page 88. So that stands to be corrected. I thank you, Registrar. So, Mr. Buric, we stop here for today. We'll give you a rest. We will continue tomorrow morning at 9.00. Is it here in this same courtroom? And hopefully we will finish with you tomorrow. You're confident that you will finish tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I'll -- yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Good evening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 13th day of September, 2005, at 9.00 a.m.
